verdict.rationale: Four authors describe the departure with concrete verbs of physical elevation parsed as passives of external agency (meaning someone or something outside the subject is doing the lifting): "he was lifted up" (ἐπήρθη, a completed past action in passive form, Acts 1:9), "he was being carried up" (ἀνεφέρετο, an ongoing past action in passive form, Luke 24:51), and "having been taken up" / "he was taken up" (ἀναλημφθεὶς and ἀνελήμφθη, a completed past participle and indicative form of the verb "to take up" (ἀναλαμβάνω), Acts 1:11 and 1 Timothy 3:16), each paired with the phrase "into heaven" (εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν). The subject is fixed as touchable flesh by Luke 24:39, where Jesus says "touch me" (ψηλαφήσατέ με) and adds "flesh and bones" (σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα). Acts 1:11 names the ascended one "this same Jesus" (οὗτος ὁ Ἰησοῦς) and equates his going with his return by "in the same manner" (οὕτως ἐλεύσεται ὃν τρόπον). Heavy eyewitness vocabulary, "while they were watching" (βλεπόντων αὐτῶν), "they were gazing intently" (ἀτενίζοντες ἦσαν), "you saw" (ἐθεάσασθε), and the named place Bethany ground the scene spatially. The one polysemous foothold (the word "to take up" or "to suppose" (ὑπολαμβάνω) used of the cloud, and the "offer up" sense of "to carry up" (ἀναφέρω) elsewhere) is overridden by the surrounding passive-motion grammar and the locative phrases (phrases naming a place).

scripture.force: Just before the ascension scene the risen Jesus says "touch me" (ψηλαφήσατέ με, a completed past action used as a command, "handle me") and "because a spirit does not have flesh and bones" (ὅτι πνεῦμα σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα οὐκ ἔχει). The lexical point (the point made by the actual words used) is that the subject who is shortly lifted up is defined here as a touchable, flesh-and-bones body, not a disembodied spirit. This fixes the referent of the later motion verbs as a physical body.

Jesus "led them out" (ἐξήγαγεν, a completed past action in active form) toward Bethany, "lifted his hands" (ἐπάρας τὰς χεῖρας, a completed past participle of the verb "to lift up" (ἐπαίρω)), and blesses them. A named place, a bodily gesture, and an active personal subject set a concrete spatial scene, not a metaphor.

While he was blessing them "he was parted from them" (διέστη, a completed past action in active form of the verb "to part" or "to separate" (διΐστημι), a verb used elsewhere only of spatial or temporal separation) and "was being carried up" (ἀνεφέρετο, parsed third person singular imperfect passive indicative, an ongoing past action in passive form, of the verb "to carry up" (ἀναφέρω)) "into heaven" (εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν). The ongoing past action in passive form depicts ongoing elevation by an external agent (someone outside the subject doing the lifting), and the locative phrase (the phrase naming a place) gives a destination. The verb "to carry up" (ἀναφέρω) is polysemous (carries multiple meanings, here "carry up" or "offer up"): it means "offer up" in Hebrews 7:27, Hebrews 9:28, Hebrews 13:15, and "lead up a mountain" in Matthew 17:1, Mark 9:2. But "into heaven" (εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν) here selects the carry-up-to-heaven sense.

"While they were watching" (βλεπόντων αὐτῶν, a grammatical bracket called a genitive absolute, a noun-phrase clock set independently of the main verb, using a present participle, an ongoing action), "he was lifted up" (ἐπήρθη, parsed third person singular aorist passive indicative, a completed past action in passive form, of the verb "to lift up" (ἐπαίρω)) and "a cloud" (νεφέλη) "took him" (ὑπέλαβεν, a completed past action in active form of the verb "to take up" or "to suppose" (ὑπολαμβάνω)) "from their eyes" (ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν). The passive "he was lifted up" (ἐπήρθη) names external agency (someone outside the subject doing the lifting), the genitive absolute (the independent noun-phrase clock just noted) fixes eyewitness observation, and the departure point is visual. The verb "to take up" or "to suppose" (ὑπολαμβάνω) is polysemous (carries multiple meanings): it means "suppose" in Luke 7:43, Acts 2:15, and "take up" in Luke 10:30. But the lift-up plus from-their-eyes context settles the physical sense.

"They were gazing intently" (ἀτενίζοντες ἦσαν, a present participle of "to gaze" (ἀτενίζω) plus an ongoing past action of "to be" (εἰμί), a construction called a periphrastic imperfect, a two-word "ongoing past" phrase) "into heaven" (εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν) as "he was going" (πορευομένου αὐτοῦ, a genitive absolute, an independent noun-phrase clock, with a present middle participle of "to go" (πορεύομαι)). The verb "to gaze intently" (ἀτενίζω) elsewhere always means "fix the eyes on something visible" (Acts 3:4, Acts 7:55, Luke 4:20), so the verb plus the present participle of "to go" (πορεύομαι) reports a sustained, observed motion of a personal subject.

The two men call the ascended one "this same Jesus who was taken up from you into heaven" (οὗτος ὁ Ἰησοῦς ὁ ἀναλημφθεὶς ἀφ ὑμῶν εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν), with "taken up" (ἀναλημφθεὶς) parsed as a completed past participle in passive form of the verb "to take up" (ἀναλαμβάνω), and say "in the same way he will come" (οὕτως ἐλεύσεται), with "he will come" (ἐλεύσεται) parsed third person singular future middle indicative, a future action of the verb "to come" (ἔρχομαι), "in the manner you saw him going into heaven" (ὃν τρόπον ἐθεάσασθε αὐτὸν πορευόμενον εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν). The demonstrative "this" (οὗτος) pins the referent to the same Jesus they watched, and "in this way" (οὕτως) plus "in the manner" (ὃν τρόπον) equates the manner of departure with the manner of return, so a non-bodily reading of the departure would also empty the promised return.

The risen Jesus tells Mary "do not cling to me" (μή μου ἅπτου, a present middle imperative, an ongoing command, of the verb "to touch" or "to cling" (ἅπτω)) "for I have not yet ascended to the Father" (οὔπω γὰρ ἀναβέβηκα πρὸς τὸν πατέρα), with "I have ascended" (ἀναβέβηκα) parsed as a perfect tense, a completed action whose result still stands, of the verb "to ascend" (ἀναβαίνω). The same dictionary form "to ascend" (ἀναβαίνω) is predicated of the touchable body Mary tries to hold, linking the touchable subject to the not-yet-completed ascent.

Jesus forecasts "the Son of Man ascending where he was before" (τὸν υἱὸν τοῦ ἀνθρώπου ἀναβαίνοντα ὅπου ἦν τὸ πρότερον, a present participle, an ongoing action, of the verb "to ascend" (ἀναβαίνω)). The same ascent verb is applied to the Son of Man before the passion, so the later Luke and Acts narration uses an already-announced motion vocabulary, not a freshly invented metaphor.

Paul cites Psalm 68:18 (the highest-voted cross-reference for this verse in the OpenBible dataset) and applies "having ascended on high" (ἀναβὰς εἰς ὕψος, a completed past participle of the verb "to ascend" (ἀναβαίνω), "having gone up to a height") to Christ. The verb "to ascend" (ἀναβαίνω) is the ordinary verb of physical going up across its 82 occurrences. The verb "to lead captive" (αἰχμαλωτεύω) is a true hapax (a word that occurs only once in the entire Bible, in this verse only), so its precise nuance cannot be triangulated from canon usage, but the ascent verb itself is unambiguous.

Paul asks what "he ascended" (τὸ ἀνέβη, a completed past action of the verb "to ascend" (ἀναβαίνω)) implies "except that he also descended" (εἰ μὴ ὅτι καὶ κατέβη, a completed past action of the verb "to descend" (καταβαίνω)) "into the lower parts of the earth" (εἰς τὰ κατώτερα μέρη τῆς γῆς). He pairs the standard up verb and down verb as a real spatial movement with a point of origin and a destination, which supports a literal reading of the ascent in verse 8.

"The one who descended" (ὁ καταβάς, a completed past participle of the verb "to descend" (καταβαίνω)) is "the same" (αὐτός) who "ascended" (ὁ ἀναβάς, a completed past participle of the verb "to ascend" (ἀναβαίνω)) "far above all the heavens" (ὑπεράνω πάντων τῶν οὐρανῶν). The locative "far above" (ὑπεράνω, a place-word) plus the plural "of the heavens" (genitive plural, the "of-X" grammatical form) assigns the ascended subject a real position, matching the Luke and Acts destination "into heaven" (εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν).

The confessional hymn runs six completed past actions in passive form in a row, "was manifested" (ἐφανερώθη), "was justified" (ἐδικαιώθη), "was seen" (ὤφθη), "was preached" (ἐκηρύχθη), "was believed on" (ἐπιστεύθη), "was taken up" (ἀνελήμφθη), with one relative subject. It opens "was manifested in flesh" (ἐφανερώθη ἐν σαρκί) and closes "was taken up in glory" (ἀνελήμφθη ἐν δόξῃ), with the closing verb parsed third person singular aorist passive indicative, a completed past action in passive form, of the verb "to take up" (ἀναλαμβάνω), the same dictionary form as Acts 1:11. The "flesh" (σάρξ) at the start and "glory" (δόξα) at the close keep the same fleshly subject in view through the taking up.

Luke opens the ascension narrative by saying the risen Jesus "presented himself alive" (παρέστησεν ἑαυτὸν ζῶντα, a present participle, an ongoing action, of the verb "to live" (ζάω)) "through forty days" (δι ἡμερῶν τεσσεράκοντα), "appearing to them" (ὀπτανόμενος). The forty-day interval is set lexically (set by the actual words used) by "forty days" (τεσσεράκοντα ἡμερῶν) inside the same narrative unit that ends with the ascension in verses 9 to 11, grounding the forty-day clause of the proposition.

complicating_texts.resolution: Jesus says "no one has ascended into heaven except the one who descended from heaven" (οὐδεὶς ἀναβέβηκεν εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν εἰ μὴ ὁ ἐκ τοῦ οὐρανοῦ καταβάς), with "has ascended" (ἀναβέβηκεν) parsed as a perfect tense, a completed action whose result still stands, of the verb "to ascend" (ἀναβαίνω). It uses the same dictionary form "to ascend" (ἀναβαίνω) as Ephesians 4:8 to 10 and is read of the Son who descended and would ascend. It limits who can ascend, the one originating from heaven, not whether a bodily ascent occurs, so it does not contradict the bodily lift in Luke and Acts.

A visionary or theological-motif reading could lean on the polysemy (the multiple-meaning quality) of the verb "to take up" or "to suppose" (ὑπολαμβάνω) used of the cloud taking him, since the verb means "suppose" in Luke 7:43 and Acts 2:15. But the governing main verb is "he was lifted up" (ἐπήρθη), the completed past action in passive form of the verb "to lift up" (ἐπαίρω), which in its 19 occurrences always means a literal raising (eyes, hands, voice, sails), and it is bracketed by "while they were watching" (βλεπόντων αὐτῶν) and "from their eyes" (ἀπὸ τῶν ὀφθαλμῶν αὐτῶν). The physical sense is therefore fixed by the surrounding grammar, not assumed.

The longer ending of Mark uses "he was taken up into heaven" (ἀνελήμφθη εἰς τὸν οὐρανὸν), lexically identical (using the same exact word) to Acts 1:11 and 1 Timothy 3:16. Even though the longer ending is text-critically secondary (a section that the manuscript evidence suggests was added later, not original), the verdict does not depend on it, since Luke 24 and Acts 1 stand independently.

variant_units_examined.note: A small group of witnesses (manuscripts) omit the phrase "and was being carried up into heaven" (καὶ ἀνεφέρετο εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν). The clause is the majority reading (the reading found in most manuscripts). Even on the shorter text, "he was parted from them" (διέστη ἀπ αὐτῶν) plus the independent Acts 1:9 to 11 parallel preserves the bodily departure frame, so the verdict holds either way.

The reading "who" (ὅς) versus "God" (θεός) at the head of the hymn changes the grammatical subject of the relative chain but does not touch "was taken up in glory" (ἀνελήμφθη ἐν δόξῃ), which is the load-bearing ascent clause (the key clause that supports the conclusion).
The longer ending of Mark is text-critically disputed (its manuscript evidence is contested) and is not required for the verdict, which rests on Luke 24 and Acts 1.

variants.note: All anchor passages lie outside the ingested ECM apparatus window (the critical edition of New Testament textual variants, here covering only 3 John 1:1 to 1:15), so no Coherence-Based Genealogical Method (a manuscript-comparison method) apparatus was examined. Variant readings are taken from the standard critical editions in shadow mode (a non-authoritative cross-check).

competing_lens_verdicts.rationale: Reads the passive motion verbs, "he was lifted up" (ἐπήρθη), "he was being carried up" (ἀνεφέρετο), "he was taken up" (ἀνελήμφθη), the locative phrase "into heaven" (εἰς τὸν οὐρανόν, a phrase naming a destination), the eyewitness verbs, and the touchable "flesh and bones" (σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα) body as a single coherent report of a visible bodily relocation. This is the strongest reading on the surface lexical data (the data of the actual words used).
Reads the ascent as the enthronement of the covenant mediator above all heavens (Ephesians 4:10), and the bodily lift is retained as the historical means of that enthronement.

Reads the ascent as the precondition for the present heavenly session and the future visible return promised in Acts 1:11, with the bodily ascent and bodily return held together by "in the manner" (ὃν τρόπον).

Treats the ascent vocabulary as a cosmological or theological metaphor of exaltation rather than a spatial relocation, leaning on the polysemy (multiple-meaning quality) of the verb "to take up" or "to suppose" (ὑπολαμβάνω) and the verb "to carry up" or "to offer up" (ἀναφέρω), and on the cloud as a theophany symbol (a symbol of God appearing). Stated in its strongest form, it argues that upward language in an ancient three-tier cosmos (a three-layer picture of the universe) need not assert literal travel. The lexical counterweight is that the governing verbs are passive verbs of physical raising bracketed by eyewitness verbs and a touchable body, which this reading must treat as figurative against the grain of their ordinary usage.

hermeneutics.notes: The verdict is stable across the grammatico-historical (plain-meaning, history-aware reading), covenantal (covenant-framework), and dispensational (dispensation-framework) lenses. The visionary lens dissents, but it does so by reading the surface motion verbs and eyewitness framing figuratively rather than by deriving its reading from them.

stem_audit.notes: The stem (the underlying yes-or-no proposition being tested) states a concrete, testable event (a bodily ascent, a forty-day interval) without encoding a tradition-specific taxonomy (without smuggling in a particular tradition's category system), so the verdict is derived from the lexical data (the data of the actual words used) rather than smuggled by the wording. Occurrence counts and morphology (the form and parsing of words) in this file were verified by direct query of the lexical store (MorphGNT parsing and GreekLemma concordance, the in-house Greek-word index) rather than taken from the capped input bundle.

lay_summary: The question is whether Christ ascended bodily into heaven forty days after his resurrection. Reading only the Greek text and standard lexical tools (tools based on the actual words used), the verbs across Luke, Acts, Ephesians, and First Timothy describe a physical event done to a physical subject. Just before the scene, Luke 24:39 has Jesus say "handle me, a spirit does not have flesh and bones" (σάρκα καὶ ὀστέα), so the one about to be lifted is a touchable body. Luke 24:51 then uses "he was being carried up" (anephereto, ἀνεφέρετο), an ongoing past action in passive form meaning he was being lifted by an outside agent, with "into heaven". Acts 1:9 uses "he was lifted up" (eperthe, ἐπήρθη), a completed past action in passive form, and notes the disciples were watching and that a cloud took him from their eyes. Acts 1:10 piles on eyewitness words: they were gazing intently into heaven as he was going. Acts 1:11 names him "this same Jesus" (οὗτος) and says he will come back "in the same manner" (ὃν τρόπον) they saw him go, so treating the departure as mere symbol would also empty the promised return. Ephesians 4 pairs the ordinary up verb "to ascend" (ἀναβαίνω) with the down verb "to descend" (καταβαίνω) to make a real spatial movement, and First Timothy 3:16 ends a chain of passives with "he was taken up in glory" (ἀνελήμφθη ἐν δόξῃ), the same verb as Acts. The forty days is fixed by Acts 1:3. There are honest soft spots a careful reader should know. The cloud verb "took him" (ὑπολαμβάνω) can elsewhere mean "suppose", and the carried-up verb (ἀναφέρω) can elsewhere mean "offer up" a sacrifice, so a few words are not decisive on their own. But the main verbs in each scene are passive verbs of physical raising, set beside watching eyes, a named place called Bethany, and a flesh-and-bones body. Across four authors the pattern is one consistent picture, and the variant readings (one clause missing in a few copies of Luke, the disputed longer ending of Mark, the "who" versus "God" reading in First Timothy 3:16) leave the verdict unchanged because Acts stands on its own.
